newsitem.title: UK: Christmas comes early for cross-Channel ferries.
newsitem.headline: Christmas comes early for cross-Channel ferries.

text.p: Christmas has come early for ferries plying the Channel after a fire in the tunnel between Britain and France unexpectedly boosted their business.
The ferry companies hastily laid on extra ships after their arch rival was hit by a fire last month on a freight train. Now business is up 50 percent.
"It has been a bumper time for us. It really is Christmas. We have stepped up a gear and hope and expect some of that market will remain with the ships," said a spokesman for P & O European Ferries
Stena Line, heading for a merger next year with P & O in the cut-throat market, agreed.
"We are very, very busy. It is more like peak season in July or August," said a spokesman.
The picture could not have been more different less than two months ago.
By the end of October, the tunnel that opened only two years ago had attracted 50 percent of the total market. P & O trailed in second with 20 percent.
Then on November 18, a fire in a lorry on a freight train seriously damaged a section of the tunnel, injuring 34 people.
The tunnel faces up to five months of repairs from the fire which burned cables and buckled track.
Trains now alternate through the other parallel tunnel. Eurostar passenger trains from London to Paris and Brussels resumed along with car-carrying Le Shuttle trains.

A spokeswoman for Eurotunnel SA plc said of Le Shuttle: "We are now working at 50 percent of capacity. At the moment it is three departures every two hours increasing to two an hour from December 30. One third of the tunnel is closed off."
"We are running a reservations only system. The feedback from customers has been very positive," she said of the tunnel, which has brought 25 percent new business on the cross-channel route.
In Calais, wines and spirits entrepreneur Dave West is the first to admit at his warehouse: "The tunnel has brought us lots of new customers and created new travellers."
"The feedback I have been getting is that people couldn't wait for it to be resumed," he said as customers queued up for cut-price wine and beer.
The ferries are the first to admit their second honeymoon cannot last.

The spokesman for Stena Line, which has been attracting an extra 7,000 passengers a day, said of the tunnel fire: "I doubt if it will have any longterm effect. If you see a car crash on your way home, you don't stop driving a car."
But what bridled him was competing on what he saw as unequal terms with Eurotunnel which renegotiated its debts with its bankers.
"You have a vast competitor with incredible capacity that doesn't obey market rules. They set prices that don't cover the costs we need to cover.
"We have got to balance the books and make a profit and Eurotunnel doesn't do that."
